design_detail: Lancet Seminar (invited clinical review; Lancet 2019;394:781–92) by five authors from Toronto, Linköping, Bogotá, Dresden and Moscow, covering diagnosis, epidemiology, genetic and other risk factors, neurobiology, treatment use and the treatment gap, psychosocial and pharmacological interventions, the care pathway from primary to specialist care, and alcohol policy, with a boxed panel on Colombia. It states a focus on developments of the past 5 years not covered by the previous Lancet Seminars (Schuckit, 2009; Connor, Haber & Hall, 2016). A boxed search strategy describes searches of Web of Science, Embase, MEDLINE and PsycINFO, plus the Cochrane Library and reference lists, for English-language publications from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2018, with preference for highly cited manuscripts; the search terms are in an online appendix that is not on file. No quantitative synthesis and no appraisal of the cited studies; 140 references. Design “narrative-review” with the editors' checklist, as the round brief directs for this Seminar.
can_establish: How five researchers in alcohol epidemiology, neurobiology and treatment summarised alcohol use disorders for clinicians in 2019: the working definition they adopt, the figures they chose for prevalence, treatment rates and treatment effects (each traceable to a cited source), and the care model and policies they recommend.
cannot_establish: Any estimate on its own authority: every figure is second-hand (WHO 2018 for prevalence, a 2004 overview for the global treatment rate, a 2010 study in the US Veterans Health Administration for prescribing rates, Jonas et al., 2014, for the naltrexone number needed to treat) and none is appraised; whether the treatments and policies it recommends work as stated (no pooling, no appraisal, the sources for Table 2 only in an appendix not on file); and anything about the management of alcohol withdrawal, which the Seminar does not review.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Evidence from the described search and from the authors' choice; highly cited manuscripts were given higher preference for inclusion (p. 781, search box).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Search box: English-language publications from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2018 in four databases, plus the Cochrane Library and reference lists of relevant manuscripts; no further criteria and no record of what was found or left out (p. 781).
sample.selection_effects: The stated window does not define the evidence base: of the 140 references, 52 are dated before 2015, 10 in 2019 and 1 is in press (editors' count from the reference list, pp. 789–792). The preference for highly cited manuscripts favours prominent findings. At least 33 references (24%) name one of the five authors, 28 of them J Rehm (editors' count; entries ending in et al. may hide more), and the four acknowledged reviewers (P Anderson, A Gual, R Room, R Wiers) are authors of further cited papers (for example refs 15, 27, 83 and 93). The primary-care figures on treatment and recognition come from a cross-sectional study led by J Rehm (ref 70), partly through the authors' own calculations.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (review). The Seminar notes that alcohol use is usually measured by self-report and recommends biomarkers of heavy drinking such as phosphatidylethanol in clinical settings, with costs and practical and ethical questions to be discussed with the patient (p. 782, Diagnosis, 6th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: No drinking amounts are defined. The Seminar's working definition of alcohol use disorder is compulsive heavy use with loss of control, which it equates with moderate-to-severe DSM-5 alcohol use disorder or ICD-11 alcohol dependence (p. 781, Diagnosis, 3rd paragraph); heavy use is not defined in grams or drinks. The prevalence figures it quotes come from WHO's 2018 report, whose case definition the Seminar does not state. The overall level of consumption in the policy correlation and the Colombian adult per-head figure (about 6 L a year) are given without saying whether litres of pure alcohol per adult are meant (p. 788).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, except that the Colombia panel reports that, according to directors of treatment institutions, most people with alcohol use disorders refused to be treated together with people who use other drugs (p. 788, Panel).

comparison.controls: Not applicable (no data of its own). Reference groups behind the figures it quotes: the population aged 15 and older (prevalence), people of high socioeconomic status (mortality ratios), the population average (life expectancy), and standardised instruments and general practitioners' identification as each other's reference (recognition in primary care).

outcomes.instruments: None of its own. Discussed: DSM-5 and ICD-11 criteria (listed in appendix pp 4–6, not on file), AUDIT and AUDIT-C for screening, phosphatidylethanol as a biomarker; treatment outcomes as reported by the cited reviews (a number needed to treat; credible intervals from a Bayesian meta-analysis).
outcomes.operationalization: Alcohol use disorder as compulsive heavy use with loss of control (p. 781); treatment success framed as reduced drinking, with abstinence said to give the largest effect on mortality (p. 782, Diagnosis, 5th paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own; all second-hand, as cited. Prevalence of alcohol use disorders in 2016, ages 15 and older: men 8.6% (95% CI 8.1–9.1), women 1.7% (1.6–1.9), total 5.1% (4.9–5.4); high-income countries 8.4% (8.0–8.9), upper-middle-income countries 5.4% (5.0–6.0) (p. 782). Life expectancy reduced by more than 20 years in Nordic register analyses (p. 782). Heritability: one Australian twin study 64%, range 40% to 70%, a meta-analysis about 50% (p. 783). ALDH2*2 carried by about 40% of East Asian people (p. 783). Treatment: 22.3% of patients with alcohol dependence in European primary care received interventions, 21.9% globally (p. 784); screening of eligible primary-care patients 5.9% (3.4–8.4) (p. 784); general practitioners identified 30.3% (27.1–33.7) of patients with an instrument-identified disorder, and instruments identified 39.9% (36.0–43.9) of patients with alcohol dependence identified by general practitioners (p. 785); cognitive bias modification: cognitive bias 0.23 (95% credible interval 0.06 to 0.41), relapse −0.27 (−0.68 to 0.22) (p. 785); naltrexone number needed to treat 12 to prevent return to heavy drinking (p. 786); medications prescribed to 0.07% overall and 5.8% of those seeking specialty treatment (p. 787); Spearman correlation between overall consumption and prevalence of alcohol use disorders 0.69 (0.60–0.76) (p. 788).
analysis.selective_reporting: An effect size is given for one approved medication only (the naltrexone number needed to treat); the strong statements in Table 2 (robust effectiveness for topiramate; sodium oxybate safe and effective; baclofen's efficacy robustly replicated in one adequately powered multicentre trial) cite sources only in the appendix, and the baclofen trial is not identified in the printed paper; no null or negative trial and no critique of the approved medications is cited; the policy section cites only supportive evidence; withdrawal management is not covered.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As presented, the cited evidence shows that alcohol use disorders affected an estimated 8.6% of men and 1.7% of women aged 15 and older worldwide in 2016 (WHO figures the authors call rough estimates); that about one in five people with alcohol dependence receive treatment (22.3% in a 2015 European primary-care study, 21.9% in a 2004 global overview); that screening in European primary care was rare (5.9% at baseline in a five-country trial); that the approved medications have meta-analytic support, with a naltrexone number needed to treat of 12 as the only effect size given; that cognitive bias modification had a small effect on cognitive bias and an uncertain effect on relapse; and that a substantial share of people recover with little or no treatment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary says these disorders are “undertreated partly because of the high stigma associated with them” and because of insufficient screening, that effective and cost-effective interventions exist, and that primary care should be responsible for most treatment, with routine screening and a stepped response (p. 781). Gaps: (1) the causal wording for stigma and screening rests on associations (p. 784) and on reasons for the treatment gap that the body says “seem to be threefold” (p. 785, Clinical presentation and treatment use, 6th paragraph); (2) the medications are said to have “solid support for modest, but clearly clinically useful effectiveness” (p. 787), and Table 2 calls topiramate robust and sodium oxybate safe and effective, without effect sizes or identified trials in the printed paper; (3) cognitive bias modification is said to have a small effect on relapse although the credible interval includes zero (p. 785); (4) the policy argument rests on an ecological correlation (0.69) whose countries, year and method are not stated and which cannot show that lowering consumption lowers the prevalence of the disorder, and minimum unit pricing is said to have promising results on the strength of one Canadian study of consumption (p. 788); (5) prescribing rates from one 2010 study in the US Veterans Health Administration are presented as general (p. 787); (6) no outcome evidence is given for the primary-care model the summary recommends (the ODHIN trial is cited only for its baseline screening rate, p. 784); (7) heritability is described as a share of disorders (p. 783). Against this, the authors call the prevalence figures rough estimates, say the cognitive bias modification evidence is not conclusive, list caveats of the neurocircuitry model including recovery without treatment, and say systematic evidence for integrated care pathways may not yet exist.

timeline.event: Miller & Wilbourne, Mesa Grande, a methodological analysis of treatment trials (ref 87): the Seminar's source for which psychosocial treatments rank among the most effective; not read here.

Kohn, Saxena, Levav & Saraceno, the treatment gap in mental health care (ref 72): source of the 21.9% global treatment figure and of the statement that the gap is larger than for any other mental disorder; not read here.
Schuckit, previous Lancet Seminar on alcohol-use disorders (ref 4).
Jonas et al., meta-analysis of pharmacotherapy in outpatient settings (ref 99): source of the naltrexone number needed to treat of 12; card being written by another reader in this round.
Rehm et al., cross-sectional study of general practitioners in six European countries (ref 70, led by the Seminar's senior author): source of the 22.3%, 30.3% and 39.9% figures; not read here.
Verhulst, Neale & Kendler, meta-analysis of twin and adoption studies (ref 39; on the project's Alcohol list, Tier B): source of the heritability of about 50%; not read here.
Connor, Haber & Hall, previous Lancet Seminar on alcohol use disorders (ref 3); Anderson et al., ODHIN five-country cluster randomised trial (ref 83), source of the 5.9% baseline screening rate.
This Seminar. No correction or published correspondence is noted in the PDF; none was searched for in this reading.
Mekonen et al., meta-analysis of treatment rates for alcohol use disorders (on the project's Alcohol list, Tier B): a more recent source for the treatment gap; not read here.
McPheeters et al., update of Jonas et al. (2014) on pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder (on the project's Alcohol list; card being written by another reader in this round).

replication.where_it_stands: A 2019 overview, not a source of primary estimates. Its prevalence figures are WHO's 2016 estimates; its treatment-gap figures date from 2004 (global) and 2015 (European primary care), and later syntheses on the project list (Mekonen et al., 2021, on treatment rates; McPheeters et al., 2023, on pharmacotherapy) should be preferred for current claims once read. It does not cover alcohol withdrawal, for which the project's withdrawal sources (Mayo-Smith, 1997; Amato et al., 2010) apply.

funding.funder: No funder of the Seminar is named. Acknowledgments: MH acknowledges funding from the Swedish Research Council (grant 2013-07434); JR and CP acknowledge funding from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Institute of Neurosciences, Mental Health and Addiction (Canadian Research Initiative in Substance Misuse [CRISM]; Ontario Node grant number SMN-13950); none of the funding parties had any role in any aspect of the paper (p. 789).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: AFC, AP and CP declare no competing interests. MH reports personal fees from BrainsWay Technologies, Indivior and Aelis Farma, and other income from Pfizer and Adial Pharmaceuticals, outside the submitted work. JR reports grants from Lundbeck and from D&A Pharma, outside the submitted work (p. 789).
funding.affiliations_note: Affiliations (p. 781): Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and University of Toronto (AFC, CP, JR); Linköping University (MH); Corporación Nuevos Rumbos, Bogotá (AP); Technische Universität Dresden and IM Sechenov First Moscow State Medical University (JR). The paper does not say whether any of the declared companies market medications it discusses (for example nalmefene in Table 1 or sodium oxybate in Table 2); this was not checked in this reading. The Seminar's working definition (heavy use as the core of the disorder) is the senior author's published position (refs 14 and 17). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For the figures, the primary sources it cites (WHO 2018; Rehm et al., 2015; Jonas et al., 2014; Harris et al., 2010) read in full, and an appraised, up-to-date synthesis of treatment rates across countries. For the central recommendation, cluster-randomised trials of routine primary-care screening with a stepped care pathway against usual care, reporting drinking, remission of the disorder and mortality.

domains.note: A search of four databases over 2015–2018 is described (strategy in an appendix not on file), which is more than many narrative reviews offer; but nothing says which retrieved papers were cited and why, highly cited manuscripts were explicitly preferred, and 52 of the 140 references predate the window and 10 postdate it (editors' count), so the evidence base was largely chosen outside the search.

No cited study is appraised. Limitations are named for the prevalence estimates (rough, culturally specific criteria), cognitive bias modification (not conclusive) and baclofen (divergent meta-analyses of small studies), but strong efficacy wording (robust, robustly replicated, safe and effective, solid support) is applied without effect sizes, and one credible interval that includes zero is read as an effect.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: At least 33 of 140 references name one of the authors (28 J Rehm); the primary-care treatment and recognition figures come from the senior author's study with the authors' own calculations, and the consumption–prevalence correlation uses an exposure dataset two authors co-wrote (Manthey et al., 2019).

Recommendations are mostly marked as such (should, might, probably), and experimental treatments are labelled Wave 3; but normative statements (primary care should be responsible for most treatment; inability to offer psychological support is no excuse not to prescribe) sit beside evidence without data, and an ecological correlation is presented as the basis of all policy measures.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the benefits and limits of the treatments and policies it recommends
domains.note: The side under-represented is evidence of limited, null or uncertain effect: no negative trial or critique of the approved medications is cited, harms appear only as table lists, the policy section cites supportive studies only, and recovery without treatment is acknowledged in two sentences (pp. 784, 787).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used (model card sc_kish_2017) and the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. A well-referenced Seminar by experienced researchers, but the evidence was selected rather than systematically gathered, and no cited study is appraised. Citable for the authors' working definition of alcohol use disorder, for how the treatment gap and the primary-care model were framed in 2019, and as a pointer to primary sources; every figure is second-hand, and claims must cite the primary source (WHO 2018 for prevalence; Rehm et al., 2015, for European primary care; Jonas et al., 2014, for the number needed to treat; Harris et al., 2010, for prescribing rates). A claim resting only on this Seminar stays at draft (METHODS §6.3). Not citable for withdrawal management, which it does not review.

key_findings.finding: Definition: diagnoses require a minimum number of operational criteria within the same 12 months; DSM-5 diagnoses the disorder when more than one criterion is met, with severity by the number met, and ICD-11 distinguishes alcohol dependence from a harmful pattern of use. Sharing reservations about DSM-5 and calling the widening gap between DSM-5 and ICD-11 problematic, the authors use alcohol use disorder for compulsive heavy use with loss of control, which they equate with moderate-to-severe DSM-5 disorder or ICD-11 dependence.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read; page checked on the rendered image)

key_findings.finding: Search: a systematic literature search per subject area of Web of Science, Embase, MEDLINE and PsycINFO for English-language publications from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2018, plus the Cochrane Library and reference lists; highly cited manuscripts were given higher preference for inclusion; search terms in appendix pp 2–3.
key_findings.note: Editors' count from the reference list (pp. 789–792): 52 of 140 references are dated before 2015, 10 in 2019 and 1 is in press. The appendix is not on file.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text and all 140 references read; appendix not on file)

key_findings.finding: Treatment goal: the authors say reduced drinking has been linked to lower mortality and is a vital goal of any treatment, and that reductions leading to abstinence give the largest effect on mortality (citing Roerecke, Gual & Rehm, 2013); brain changes caused by alcohol are described as partly reversible after abstinence.

Prevalence in 2016 (adults aged 15 and older, citing WHO's 2018 global status report and Rehm & Shield, 2019): men 8.6% (95% CI 8.1–9.1), women 1.7% (1.6–1.9), total 5.1% (4.9–5.4); men's prevalence five times women's, with signs of the gap narrowing; highest in high-income (8.4%, 8.0–8.9) and upper-middle-income countries (5.4%, 5.0–6.0). The authors say these survey-based figures should be considered rough estimates because several criteria are culturally specific.
key_findings.note: Figure 1 is a world map of 2016 prevalence by country with bands from 0.0–2.0% to 15.1–21.2%; country values were not extracted, and the caption gives no source (the text attributes it to WHO 2018). The case definition behind the WHO figures is not stated in the Seminar.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read; Figure 1 seen on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Mortality: excess mortality of people with alcohol use disorders (mainly through conditions such as cirrhosis or injury) does not appear in burden-of-disease reports, where alcohol poisoning is the main cause of death listed under these disorders, but only in special analyses; register analyses in Nordic countries show life expectancy reduced by more than 20 years from the population average (citing Westman et al., 2015).

Socioeconomic gradient: people of low socioeconomic status are at higher risk of the disorders and at least twice as likely to die from them and from prolonged heavy drinking as people of high status (citing Probst et al., 2015); the low-versus-high ratio is higher for alcohol-attributable causes than for all causes, which the authors read as an interaction and as more harm per litre in people of low status.

Heritability: an Australian twin study estimated 64%; twin and adoption studies of the past 35 years report 40% to 70% with no sex difference; a meta-analysis (Verhulst et al., 2015) gives about 50%, possibly an underestimate; concordance rates below 50% are taken to show that environmental factors and gene–environment interactions also contribute.
key_findings.locator: Genetics and other risk factors, 1st paragraph (begins p. 782; figures on p. 783)
key_findings.note: The text says “about 50% of alcohol use disorders are heritable” (reporting issue 6).

key_findings.finding: Genes: carriers of ALDH2*2, especially homozygotes, accumulate acetaldehyde when they drink (flushing, headache, sweating, tachycardia, nausea, vomiting), which protects against the disorder; the variant is carried by about 40% of East Asian people and is rare in European people; ADH variants such as ADH1B*2 are also protective; the largest genome-wide meta-analysis of AUDIT scores (2019) found ten risk loci.
key_findings.locator: Genetics and other risk factors, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Environmental and family risk factors named: permissive cultures with cheap, available alcohol and advertising, positive expectancies, poor family support, conduct and mood disorders, low self-control, perceived peer drinking, low parental monitoring, parental drinking and favourable parental attitudes; a 2018 prospective cohort found parental supply of alcohol associated with adolescent drinking, alcohol-related harms and symptoms of the disorder.
key_findings.locator: Genetics and other risk factors, 5th–6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Neurobiology: alcohol facilitates GABA-A and inhibits NMDA receptor signalling, suppressing nervous-system excitability, which rebounds during withdrawal; higher than normal stimulation and lower than normal sedation predict progression to the disorder (citing King et al., 2016). The authors note caveats of the three-stage neurocircuitry model: it ignores the recovery phase, structural and functional brain changes may reverse after abstinence, and a substantial proportion of people recover with no or minimal treatment.
key_findings.locator: Genetics and other risk factors, 7th paragraph (p. 783) and 10th paragraph (p. 784)

key_findings.finding: Treatment use: in a study of more than 13 000 patients and 358 general practitioners in six European countries, 22.3% of patients identified with alcohol dependence received interventions; the most recent global overview gave 21.9%, and some countries such as the USA were lower; the authors infer a treatment gap larger than for any other mental disorder.
key_findings.locator: Clinical presentation and treatment use, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The European figure is from Rehm et al. (2015, ref 70); the global figure and the comparison with other disorders are from Kohn et al. (2004, ref 72), 15 years before the Seminar (reporting issues 1 and 2).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text and reference list read)

key_findings.finding: Stigma: compared with people not in treatment, people in treatment show more social disintegration, drinking, comorbidity and functional loss; fear of stigma has been associated with less access to treatment; stigma towards alcohol use disorders has not improved over time while stigma towards mental disorders generally has; high stigma has been recorded among health professionals.
key_findings.locator: Clinical presentation and treatment use, 2nd–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Screening: no systematic screening exists in primary care in most countries; in five European jurisdictions, including two with the highest screening rates (Catalonia and England), 5.9% (95% CI 3.4–8.4) of eligible adult patients were screened during a 4-week baseline period (ODHIN trial, Anderson et al., 2016).
key_findings.locator: Clinical presentation and treatment use, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Recognition in primary care (six-country European study): general practitioners rely on drinking level and signs such as breath, red eyes and raised liver enzymes rather than criteria; they identified 30.3% (95% CI 27.1–33.7) of patients with an alcohol use disorder identified by standardised instruments, while the instruments identified 39.9% (36.0–43.9) of patients with alcohol dependence identified by the general practitioners (authors' own calculations from Rehm et al., 2015).
key_findings.locator: Clinical presentation and treatment use, 5th paragraph (begins p. 784; figures on p. 785)

key_findings.finding: Psychosocial treatment: citing Miller and Wilbourne (2002), brief counselling, motivational enhancement therapy, the community reinforcement approach, guided self-change, behaviour contracting and social skills training were among the ten most effective interventions; the authors say little has changed, that specific well-defined therapies are more effective than unstructured therapist–patient interaction, and that their effective elements have not been identified.

Cognitive bias modification (the most comprehensive review, a Bayesian individual-participant meta-analysis, Boffo et al., 2019): effect on cognitive bias 0.23 (95% credible interval 0.06 to 0.41) and on relapse −0.27 (−0.68 to 0.22), none on substance use; the authors call the evidence, when added to other treatments, not conclusive and in need of more rigorous randomised trials.
key_findings.note: The relapse interval includes zero although the text describes a small effect on relapse; the scale of both estimates is not stated (reporting issue 3).

key_findings.finding: Approved medications (Wave 1: disulfiram, naltrexone oral or depot, nalmefene, acamprosate) all have meta-analytic support and different indications: disulfiram only under supervision; naltrexone and nalmefene mainly prevent relapse to heavy drinking and could serve a goal of controlled drinking; acamprosate promotes abstinence in severe disorder. The authors say their effect sizes resemble those of common medical treatments, citing a number needed to treat of 12 for naltrexone to prevent return to heavy drinking (Jonas et al., 2014).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read; Table 1 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Table 1 safety notes: a disulfiram–ethanol reaction may be an emergency, so disulfiram can sustain abstinence but not reduce drinking; naltrexone and nalmefene can block opioid analgesics and precipitate opioid withdrawal; acamprosate does not undergo first-pass metabolism and can be used in liver disease; listed adverse effects include hepatotoxicity, neuropathy, psychosis and optic neuritis for disulfiram, and diarrhoea, pruritus, rash and altered libido for acamprosate.
key_findings.note: Table 1 also has a dosage column, not extracted (the project reports no dosing).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (Table 1 read on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Off-label medications (Wave 2: baclofen, gabapentin, ondansetron, sodium oxybate, topiramate, varenicline) are said to have meta-analytic support. Topiramate has perhaps the strongest support but needs careful titration and causes early cognitive side-effects, so stays a specialist treatment; baclofen meta-analyses, mostly of small studies, diverge, but efficacy was robustly replicated in one adequately powered multicentre trial, with tolerance and dose escalation risking serious adverse events; sodium oxybate was safe and effective in severe dependence but has high potential for non-medical use and is reserved for specialist settings.
key_findings.note: Table 2's sources are only in the appendix (pp 8–9), not on file; the baclofen trial is not identified in the printed paper. A dose mentioned for gabapentin was not extracted.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (Table 2 read on the rendered page; appendix not on file)

key_findings.finding: Prescribing: several medications have solid support for modest but clinically useful effectiveness, yet are prescribed to an estimated 0.07% of patients with alcohol use disorders overall and 5.8% of those seeking specialty treatment (citing Harris et al., 2010, on the US Veterans Health Administration); the authors judge wider use of existing treatments the greatest short-term opportunity.
key_findings.note: The source is one health system in one country (reporting issue 4).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text and reference list read)

key_findings.finding: Care pathway: primary care should be the entry point and the site of most treatment, with regular checks of drinking like blood-pressure checks, brief advice first, then lifestyle interventions, then psychological and pharmacological treatment; specialist referral when drinking stays high or comorbidity exceeds primary care; inability to offer psychological support should not stop prescribing. Figure 2 sets out a stepped model from screening of all adults to specialised care. An important proportion of these disorders improve without formal intervention (citing Walters, 2000).
key_findings.locator: Acute and long-term management, 1st–4th paragraphs; Figure 2
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text read; Figure 2 read on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal is not reviewed: it appears only as the withdrawal or negative-affect stage of the neurobiological model and as rebound excitability (p. 783), and detoxification only as an option “if needed” in Figure 2 and in a pointer to guidelines from NICE (2011) and Rolland et al. (2016) (p. 787). No evidence on withdrawal management is given.
key_findings.locator: Genetics and other risk factors, 7th–8th paragraphs (p. 783); Acute and long-term management, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2 (p. 787)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text and reference list read)

key_findings.finding: Experimental medications (Wave 3): neurokinin-1 antagonism reduced alcohol self-administration in rodents and stress-induced craving in patients, but industry programmes stopped after depression trials; mifepristone reduced cue-induced craving and drinking in a small 1-week laboratory study in men; a ghrelin antagonist has so far proved safe; a κ-opioid antagonist trial began in 2019 (NCT03852628).

Policy: the authors base restrictions on availability, marketing bans and taxation on the association between overall consumption and the prevalence of alcohol use disorders, a Spearman correlation of 0.69 (95% CI 0.60–0.76) based on WHO's 2018 report and Manthey et al. (2019); minimum unit pricing (several Eastern European countries, Scotland, some Canadian provinces) is said to have promising results, citing one Saskatchewan study; these policies are called highly cost-effective (citing Chisholm et al., 2018).
key_findings.locator: The role of the wider environment and alcohol policy, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (the 3rd begins p. 788)
key_findings.note: The number of countries, the year and the method of the correlation are not stated (reporting issue 5).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (all text and reference list read)

key_findings.finding: Colombia panel: adult per-head consumption about 6 L a year; prevalence of alcohol use disorders 7% in 2016; Law 1566 of 2012 made substance use a public-health matter and gave a right to free state-of-the-art treatment, but took 5 years to implement because private institutions wanted guaranteed reimbursement; as of May 2019, facilities offering inpatient treatment of up to 90 days for alcohol use disorders only remained almost empty, according to directors of treatment institutions.
key_findings.locator: Panel: Hazardous alcohol use and alcohol use disorders in Colombia
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf (panel read on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Declarations: AFC, AP and CP no competing interests; MH personal fees from BrainsWay Technologies, Indivior and Aelis Farma and other income from Pfizer and Adial Pharmaceuticals; JR grants from Lundbeck and D&A Pharma; all outside the submitted work. Funders (Swedish Research Council; Canadian Institutes of Health Research, CRISM Ontario Node) had no role in the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the low treatment rate in the European countries “is not common in other regions”, then that the global rate was almost the same (21.9%) and some countries' rates lower.
reporting_issues.page: p. 784, Clinical presentation and treatment use, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The sentence contradicts the evidence that follows it (probably “not uncommon” was meant); claims should rest on the figures, not on that sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: The “most recent overview” of global treatment (21.9%) and the statement that the treatment gap is larger than for any other mental disorder both rest on Kohn et al. (2004), published 15 years before the Seminar.
reporting_issues.page: p. 784, Clinical presentation and treatment use, 1st paragraph; reference 72
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure should be dated when cited, or replaced by a later synthesis (Mekonen et al., 2021, is on the project list).

reporting_issues.issue: Cognitive bias modification is said to have a small effect on relapse, but the 95% credible interval (−0.68 to 0.22) includes zero; the scale of the estimates is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The data cited do not show an effect on relapse; claims should say the effect on relapse is uncertain and take the scale from Boffo et al. (2019).

reporting_issues.issue: Prescribing rates of 0.07% overall and 5.8% in specialty treatment are presented as general estimates but come from one 2010 study in the US Veterans Health Administration; the denominator of the overall figure is not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures describe one health system around 2010; the primary paper must be read before they are used, and they should not be cited as a global rate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Spearman correlation of 0.69 (0.60–0.76) between overall consumption and prevalence of alcohol use disorders is given without the number of countries, the year or how it was computed; it combines WHO's 2018 data with an exposure dataset co-authored by two of the authors.
reporting_issues.page: p. 788, The role of the wider environment and alcohol policy, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: An ecological correlation, not reproducible from the paper, and unable to show that lowering consumption lowers prevalence; whether any country's prevalence was itself estimated from consumption, which would build in part of the correlation, cannot be checked from the Seminar.

reporting_issues.issue: Heritability is described as “about 50% of alcohol use disorders are heritable”, and concordance rates below 50% are cited without saying which concordance (for example identical twins) is meant.
reporting_issues.page: p. 783, Genetics and other risk factors, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Heritability is the share of variation in liability attributable to genetic differences in a population, not a share of disorders; claims should use the meta-analysis's own wording (Verhulst et al., 2015).

reporting_issues.issue: Recognition in primary care: the first figure (30.3%) is given for patients with an alcohol use disorder and the second (39.9%) for patients with alcohol dependence, although the cited study is titled as a study of alcohol dependence; the second figure is the authors' own calculation, method not given.
reporting_issues.page: p. 785, Clinical presentation and treatment use, 5th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The construct behind each figure must be checked in Rehm et al. (2015) before either is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Minimum unit pricing is said to have promising results in several Eastern European countries, Scotland and some Canadian provinces, but the only citation for the results is a study of consumption in Saskatchewan (Stockwell et al., 2012); Scotland's results are not cited.
reporting_issues.page: p. 788, The role of the wider environment and alcohol policy, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement rests on one provincial study of consumption, not of harm; the Scottish evaluation on the project list (Wyper et al., 2023) is needed for claims about Scotland.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists psychosis twice among disulfiram's adverse effects, and the text calls disulfiram “a dehydrogenase inhibitor” where Table 1 says aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor.

Typesetting errors: “alcohol use s” (p. 782); “Known personality risk factors for might be” and a garbled sentence on polygenic risk scores and DSM-IV alcohol dependence scores (p. 783); “alcohol cues inpatients” (p. 785); “Alcoholic Anonymous” and “najor” in the panel (p. 788).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, except that the polygenic-risk sentence on p. 783 cannot be read as printed and should not be cited without the primary paper (Li et al., 2017, ref 51).
